The intensity of wave X is I.

hints: Notice the peak values on the displacement / cm axis: wave X peaks near $0.40 \text{ cm}$ and wave Y peaks near $0.75 \text{ cm}$ - these are the amplitudes.
Check the distance / cm axis for wavelength: both waves start at $0$ and return to zero at $14 \text{ cm}$, so both have the same wavelength and, in the same medium, the same frequency.
Connect amplitude to intensity with $I \propto A^2$ for constant frequency, so you need to square the ratio of the two peak displacements.
walkthrough: Read amplitude $A$ as maximum displacement from the graph. Wave X reaches about $0.40 \text{ cm}$ and wave Y reaches about $0.75 \text{ cm}$.
Read wavelength from the displacement-distance graph. Both waves complete one full oscillation between $0$ and $14 \text{ cm}$, so $\lambda_X = \lambda_Y = 14 \text{ cm}$.
Since they are the same type in the same medium, wave speed $v$ is the same, so $f = v/\lambda$ is the same for X and Y. Therefore only amplitude affects the intensity ratio.
Use $I \propto A^2 f^2$, so with equal $f$, $I_Y/I_X = (A_Y/A_X)^2$.
Substitute the amplitudes: $I_Y/I = (0.75/0.40)^2 \approx (1.875)^2 \approx 3.5$. The unit $\text{cm}$ cancels in the ratio, leaving a pure number times $I$.

A.explanation: This is about $1/3.5$ and would result from inverting the intensity ratio as $I_X/I_Y$ instead of $I_Y/I_X$.

B.explanation: This is about $1/1.9$ and would result from inverting the amplitude ratio and not squaring it correctly.

C.explanation: This is the amplitude ratio $A_Y/A_X$ about $1.9$, but intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so this omits the squaring.

D.explanation: The amplitude ratio squared is about $1.875^2 \approx 3.5$, which gives $I_Y \approx 3.5I$ for the same frequency.
